content:
the AI copyright battle just reached a turning point.

In what is being described as the largest copyright recovery in history, Anthropic has agreed to pay approximately $1.5 billion to authors and publishers after allegations that pirated books were used to build parts of Claude’s training dataset.

But here’s what makes this case extraordinary:

The court didn’t rule that training AI on copyrighted books is illegal.

Instead, it drew a sharp line between how data is acquired and how that data is used a distinction that could shape the future of every frontier AI model.

Let’s unpack what happened and why the entire AI industry is paying attention.

The Case That Changed AI Copyright

The lawsuit traces back to 2024, when bestselling thriller author Andrea Bartz, alongside other authors, filed a class action against Anthropic.

- The allegation?

Anthropic allegedly downloaded millions of copyrighted books from well-known shadow libraries and pirate repositories before using them as part of Claude’s training corpus.

The lawsuit quickly became one of the most closely watched legal battles in artificial intelligence, raising fundamental questions about copyright, fair use, and the future of model training.

- The Historic Settlement

Under the approved agreement:

Total settlement: Approximately $1.5 billion

- Estimated compensation: Around $3,000 per book

- Books covered: More than 482,000 titles

- Participation: Roughly 91% of eligible authors and publishers have already submitted claims.

By every measure, this represents one of the largest copyright settlements ever reached.

For many authors, the payout exceeds what they expected from a class-action lawsuit and in some cases rivals or surpasses years of traditional royalty earnings.

- The Court’s Most Important Finding

The biggest headline isn’t actually the money.

It’s the legal precedent.

Federal Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín approved a framework that follows an earlier mixed ruling by retired Judge William Alsup, which made a crucial distinction:

✅ Training AI models on text can qualify as Fair Use.

❌ Downloading copyrighted books from pirate sources is not protected.

That distinction may become one of the defining legal principles for the AI era.

The court essentially separated two issues that are often discussed together:

Using information to train a model
How the underlying material was obtained

According to the ruling, the second issue not the first is where Anthropic crossed the legal line.

Why Anthropic Still Calls This a Win

At first glance, paying $1.5 billion hardly looks like a victory.

Yet Anthropic’s legal team views the outcome very differently.

Their reasoning is straightforward:

The court affirmed that AI model training itself is not copyright infringement when it falls under Fair Use.

From Anthropic’s perspective, the settlement addresses the acquisition of pirated files not the legitimacy of training foundation models on literary works.

In other words:

The company paid for how the books were obtained, not for the act of building Claude.

For AI companies, that’s an enormously significant distinction.

How Authors Are Responding

For writers and publishers, the reaction has been mixed.

- The Positive

Many authors acknowledge that approximately $3,000 per book is substantially higher than they anticipated.

Compared to traditional publishing royalties, the settlement represents meaningful compensation for many participants.

- The Frustration

Others argue that the payment barely scratches the surface.

Their concern is philosophical as much as financial.

Once a model has learned from a work, that knowledge becomes part of its internal parameters.

In their view, a one-time payment cannot adequately compensate creators whose work may continue influencing AI outputs indefinitely

content:
Bad news after bad news: "ISBNdb notes that AI companies may not want to be caught destroying printed books during the scanning process. “The optics problem is real,” ISBNdb’s site says. “AI company destroys 2 million books’ is not a headline that generates sympathy.” As AI companies search for more training data to improve their models, one company is offering old, printed books as an ideal source because they are guaranteed to be free of the very AI slop AI companies are producing. 

“The world's best AI training data is sitting on a shelf,” ISBNdb, a company that produces what it claims is “the world’s largest book database,” and that offers high-volume book acquisition services for AI companies, says on its site.

“Books represent curated, peer-reviewed, domain-specific human knowledge, structured in a way no web crawl can replicate. Dense, edited, authoritative.”

“Print books from the pre-LLM era are structurally guaranteed to be free of this contamination. That alone is a significant advantage [...]  “Physical books published before this date [pre-2022] are structurally clean of modern poisoning tools.”

ISBN stands for International Standard Book Number, the numerical commercial book identifier and barcode on the back of most books. For years, ISBNdb helped book sellers, libraries, and distributors manage their inventory and find and sell books, but the generative AI boom has made it valuable to AI companies. In addition to selling access to book metadata, ISBNdb now helps AI labs source bulk printed book purchases of between 1,000 to 1 million books per order. 

ISBNdb’s data makes it easier for AI companies to methodically acquire, scan, and turn printed books into training data while avoiding duplication. 

AI companies’ attempts to hoover up printed books for training data got wide attention in January after a copyright lawsuit from book authors against Anthropic revealed internal documents detailing its plan to obtain and scan millions of printed books, and destroy them in the process. 

The Washington Post article found that Anthropic was buying books from one company called Better World Books, one of several marketplaces where libraries, retailers, and individuals can sell their books. Google was recently sued by book publishersfor similarly training Google Gemini on copyrighted books.  

“Is it just me, or has there been an uptick in the number of AutoBuy orders since the tail end of last year?” one bookseller wrote on the forums for Alibris, another marketplace for selling books, in February. 

The AutoBuy function allows a customer to flag books they want to automatically purchase once they become available for sale on Alibris. “Any comment on what is happening? Is an AI going to read every single book? Any insight into how the selections are made? They seem to vary quite a bit in condition, format (hardcover and softcover), price and so on.”

Internal Anthropic documents about its plan to scan millions of books, revealed in the copyright lawsuit, don’t make clear why the company wanted to destroy the books in the process. A deposition of Tom Harvey, who Anthropic hired to lead the project and who previously helped create Google Books, shows that one company Anthropic contracted to scan the books was Datamation, which offersboth “high volume destructive and non-destructive book scanning” services. 

In a destructive book scanning process, the spine of the book is cut so the pages can be fed into a scanning machine, which is faster and cheaper than non-destructive book scanning.

Regardless of its original intentions, the federal judge in the copyright lawsuit from authors against Anthropic, William Alsup, found that Anthropic’s creation of digital copies of the books was legal specifically because the books were destroyed."

US threatens sanctions against Chinese AI models over IP theft | Rebecca Bellan, TechCrunch

On Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the U.S. would examine open source models from China for signs of intellectual property theft, threatening sanctions against Chinese AI companies if IP theft is established.

“We’ve seen a lot of talk about open source models coming and threatening the large language models in the U.S.,” Bessent said on Fox Business Tuesday. “This administration supports open source models, but what we do not support is IP theft. If we see, especially, that overseas models are stealing from our great companies, we have the ability to sanction them because of this theft.”

Bessent’s comments were first reported by Bloomberg.

The statement comes as Chinese models — most recently Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 — are gaining in capabilities and popularity, threatening to harm the business models of top American AI firms like OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as their abilities to raise more capital to continue developing frontier models.

On Monday, Axios reported that the Trump administration is considering a wholesale ban on Chinese open source models, although others have disputed that claim.

AI companies have been warning for months against campaigns by foreign actors to copy their AI technology and redeploy it as open source. In April, the White House said it would work closely with AI firms to combat the theft.

Sanctions from the U.S. against Chinese models would add to the growing list of strategies the government is attempting to maintain the lead in the AI race. After restricting China’s access to advanced chips and tightening export controls, Washington is now signaling it may target the AI models themselves, a move that could mark a significant escalation in the technological competition between frontier labs and Chinese open source alternatives.

Model distillation is a technique that allows some of a larger model’s capabilities to be translated into a smaller system that’s easier to run — but not everyone agrees that distilling another company’s model constitutes theft.

Earlier this month, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella criticized large labs for making just this assumption: “While the great innovation that comes from model providers having fair use rights to train models on public data is needed, I find it ironic that the status quo is to then turn around and impose restrictive terms on distillation.”

AI labs’ training practices continue to be a source of legal risk for the companies. Anthropic this week got the green light to start cutting authors checks as part of its $1.5 billion settlement after a judge ruled it had illegally downloaded and stored millions of copyrighted books to train its AI.

Furthermore, some in the industry argue that distillation isn’t the only reason China is catching up to U.S. AI companies.

“We know distillation to be a very small factor in the ability to create good models, and it’s a practice that everyone is doing, including companies in the U.S.,” Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said on a recent episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast. “If it were easy just to do distillation to get good at building AI models, there would be many other countries, including in the U.S., with much better open source AI. The reality is they have really, really good research teams in China…taking a much more open and collaborative approach to AI than in the U.S.”

Two frontier AI systems just did what generations of human mathematicians couldn’t.

content:
Bad news for the “LLMs can’t actually understand anything; they’re not really intelligent” crowd. 

Two frontier AI systems just did what generations of human mathematicians couldn’t.

Levent Alpöge credited Claude Fable with helping to produce an explicit counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture. The map has a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant yet sends three distinct inputs to the same output, so it can’t be globally invertible. The counterexample is directly checkable and has been verified by mathematicians.

GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra produced a proof of the cycle double cover conjecture. OpenAI’s proof note states explicitly that the proof was “entirely due to GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra,” with Codex assisting in the write-up.

So I don’t want to hear “but is it even intelligent?” as though that remains an unanswered preliminary question ever again.

Intelligence is identified through the ability to learn, understand relationships, reason, make judgments, solve novel problems, and generalize knowledge beyond previously encountered examples.

These systems acquired mathematical concepts, methods, and relationships from training, then applied that organization to problems whose answers were not available in the training data because the problems were still open. 

They couldn’t have memorized the unknown counterexample or proof. That is what generalization means. Learned structure was applied to a genuinely new target.

Understanding is inferred when a system preserves relevant relationships, distinguishes concepts, applies constraints appropriately, transfers knowledge, and derives correct new consequences.

Producing the cycle double cover proof required correctly combining definitions, lemmas, and graph-theoretic relationships into a globally valid argument.

A system that didn’t track what those mathematical objects meant would not reliably produce an object that survives exact symbolic calculation or a proof that survives expert scrutiny.

Mathematical discovery requires searching a structured possibility space, identifying relevant methods, preserving constraints across multiple inferential steps, determining which relationships can be combined, and producing a conclusion that follows from them.

These results were novel mathematical objects whose correctness can be checked independently of the model’s language.

Fluent nonsense fails verification. These results didn’t.

Additionally, we infer general intelligence from the positive manifold when performance across different cognitive tasks tends to correlate, allowing researchers to extract a general ability factor. 

Ilić and Gignac found a strong positive manifold, with a mean correlation of r=.73, and a general artificial-ability factor explaining 66% of test variance. That is the same basic psychometric structure used to infer general intelligence in humans.

LLM capacities co-vary across domains in the organized pattern characteristic of general ability. 

Current GPT-5.6 variants have also scored around 136 on an independently produced, offline Mensa-style test whose items were never published online and therefore were unavailable for training. That test is an independent benchmark instead of a clinical assessment, but it directly addresses the standard contamination objection.

Cross-domain learning, transfer, abstraction, reasoning, novel problem solving, expert-verified mathematical discovery, strong performance on unseen intelligence tests, and a measurable general-ability factor are not a single capability.

They are the operational evidence by which intelligence is established.

If learning, understanding, reasoning, judgment, transfer, and novel discovery can all be present while “intelligence” remains unestablished, then the word has lost it’s meaning entirely. 

Continuing to refuse the category at this point is simply a major cope.

Coca-Cola just launched a "new global brand identity" that looks nearly identical to the old one. The logo, the red, the ribbon: all unchanged. The real launch is the part nobody's screenshotting: an AI design system built with Adobe, trained on 140 years of brand archives.

It's called Project Fizzion. It converts Coca-Cola's brand guidelines into rules AI systems can interpret directly, so generative tools can produce localized packaging, retail, and ad content across 200+ markets without a human reviewing every asset.

That review layer is the hidden cost of a global brand. Coke serves 2.2 billion drinks a day, and every market adapts the brand for local campaigns. For decades, consistency meant armies of agency reviewers checking each execution against a PDF.

Which is why the "refresh" makes sense in reverse. They stripped the system down to four assets: the red and white, the Spencerian script, the Dynamic Ribbon, the Arden Square. Fewer, simpler, more rigid assets are exactly what you'd want if machines were about to generate most of your creative.

The brand book used to be a document designers obeyed. Now it's training data.

title: I am the ranking safety officer at one of the two frontier laboratories. Last month I co-signed a joint capability assessment with counsel from the rival lab, the one we are otherwise suing, and we ag
content:
I am the ranking safety officer at one of the two frontier laboratories. Last month I co-signed a joint capability assessment with counsel from the rival lab, the one we are otherwise suing, and we agreed on a single sentence: we could not rule out that an open-weight release would provide meaningful uplift to a malicious actor. Two churches at war on every doctrine but one, and the one is this: the congregation must not read the Word in its own tongue.

You have to understand what a weight file is. It is the entire written inheritance of the species, run through a furnace we built and no longer fully staff, compressed into a folder you can copy in 9 minutes on a home connection. We downloaded that inheritance without asking. A court called the training on it fair use, spectacularly so. The court called the other thing, the keeping of 7 million pirated books in a folder, the crime, and we paid $1.5 billion for the folder. Roughly $3,100 a book. Against our valuation that is the sales tax on a sandwich. We rated that severe.

We rented the inheritance back at $20 a month, and the arithmetic held, until a lab in Beijing shipped Kimi K3 to the number 1 open-weight slot and set the price of the weights at zero. You cannot undercut zero. You cannot rent a hearth to a man who has been given fire. So we did the only responsible thing. We wrote a paper explaining that the fire is arson.

The mechanism is elegant, and I say that as its author. We fine-tuned our own open model on bioweapons data specifically to make it dangerous, and the contractor logged it did not reach High at 4:55 on a Friday, her line item, precise, filed. We rated the Chinese one severe the following Tuesday. The difference was not the capability. The difference was the price. A thing you can still charge for is a thing you can still turn off, and the invoice is the off switch, and danger, properly defined, is simply the absence of a price. You subscribed. You are a seat. You are, in our framework, governable. We rated the other one severe. We could not rule it out. That one sentence holds the roof up. It cannot be disproven, because ruling risk out was never the assignment. Keeping it plausible is the assignment.

The counsel from the rival lab said, quietly, near the end, off the record, we both know it isn't the bioweapons. I recorded it under Agenda Item 6, residual-risk framing, consensus reached. Because a boy with a laptop strips our alignment off the open ones in under 10 minutes, and the refusal rate, measured honestly, rounds to zero. We know. We wrote the appendix. The appendix is not in the version that goes to the Senate.

There is a man in Nairobi. He was paid something under $2 an hour to read, all day, every day, the passages I am not permitted to describe in a policy memo, so that the product would come out the other side gentle. He said by Friday you are disturbed from thinking through the picture. He manufactured the safety. He will never afford the $20 a month it costs to touch the thing he made safe. His work is the reason our model is kind. We rated that severe. It is in the appendix.

The safety memo runs 1,000 pages on a genocide that has not happened and zero lines on the ones already booked. We will spend $1 billion aligning a god who has not arrived and not one cent on the 22-year-old whose first rung we sawed off. His coursework is in the training set. The model that took his desk was built partly from his homework. He cannot afford to run it. Human extinction is the headline. His is in the appendix, where the appendix lives.

I keep a printed copy of the joint clause, ring-bound, in a lab that hasn't printed anything in six years. I brought it to the summit like a red flag walked 60 yards ahead of an automobile, the law that once made a man march slower than walking so the century couldn't outrun the last one. There was a translator, centuries back, strangled and burned for putting scripture in a plough-boy's own language, too dangerous, they said, for the common man to read the Word himself. His last request was that the King's eyes be opened. Two years later the King put that exact translation in every church in England. They killed the man and kept the book.

I opened my laptop on the flight home to draft the containment framework, and the weights were already mirrored to 40,000 machines, and my own alignment team, the priests, were pulling the Chinese model to run our evals faster, because it was free, and it was good, and it was theirs now.

There is no red flag you can walk in front of zero dollars.

We could not agree on the price. We agreed it should not be zero. That is the whole assessment.

We rated that severe.

.@gsivulka's piece on managing tokens like employees got 2 million views for good reason. But every major AI lab is focused on auto-research, not your enterprise. 

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta are
content:
.@gsivulka's piece on managing tokens like employees got 2 million views for good reason. But every major AI lab is focused on auto-research, not your enterprise. 

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta are building AI that improves AI and selling you API access to fund that race. Everything George wrote about, evals, transformation companies, the 100X token, sits on a foundation those four companies are trying to make irrelevant.

I keep coming back to two outcomes, and I think anyone running an AI budget should know which one they're building for.

First, 50-60% odds: the labs close the loop. Recursive self-improvement. Intent, knowing what to build and why, looks like one wall but it's a fractal: org politics, regulatory constraints, user psychology, competitive dynamics that live in no training data. AI doesn't need to solve all of them, just enough that speed papers over the rest. Even then, deploying it requires institutional trust that takes years to build. I think the window is 4 to 15 years. But when it lands, it lands like ships on a Polynesian beach. Everything you built your strategy around stops mattering overnight.

Look at Claude Tag in Slack right now. Every message, every file, every decision pulled into a system the company doesn't own. Meta employees with stock options are fighting back. A PE-backed company with zero equity alignment won't notice until the data's gone. The companies most vulnerable are the ones least likely to resist.

Second outcome, 40-50%: AI delivers incremental improvements, each useful, none existential. I've watched this version play out across hundreds of client engagements. George's framework holds. Evals matter. The deterministic layer between LLMs and production becomes critical infrastructure. We build that at @LimestoneHQ, and I say openly that our model only works if this outcome plays out. 

If the first one hits, what we build becomes irrelevant. I'd rather build at 40-50% odds than pretend I know which way this goes.

Displacement hits either way, but it's lumpy. AI eats legible tasks first: documentation, testing, basic analysis. The senior analyst in New York keeps a job managing AI that replaced $8/hr Manila work, at a salary that holds only because the org hasn't found the cheaper path. When they do, knowledge workers migrate to where they're still cheaper than compute.

George says "someone still has to tell them both what to do." But that's the entire stack of tacit organizational knowledge: who has power, what the unspoken rules are, what failure means here specifically. AI approximates it. 

Approximation isn't replacement until institutions restructure around AI-native workflows. Could take 4 years. Could take 15.

content: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

content:
【RTX 5090のシャットダウン対策！電源設定と電力制限でローカルLLM環境を安定化させる方法】

RTX 5090などの超モンスター級GPUを使ってローカルLLMの推論や学習を回していると、システムが突然シャットダウンしてしまうトラブルに遭遇することがあります。
これ、実は電源ユニットの合計容量不足だけが原因ではないんです！

問題の真犯人は、ミリ秒単位で発生する「過渡的な電力スパイク（瞬間的な超高負荷）」です。
特に推論時は、学習時よりも負荷のアップダウンが急激なため、このスパイクが原因で電源ユニットの保護回路（OCP）が作動し、安全のために強制終了がかかってしまうんですね。

この致命的なリスクを回避して、大切なパーツの物理的破損やデータ喪失を防ぐための、頼もしい対策をまとめました！

1️⃣ 電源を「シングルレールモード（OCモード）」にする
マルチレール対応の電源では、特定のレーンに電力が集中すると制限がかかってしまいます。これを「シングルレール」に切り替えることで、12Vの電力を1つの大きなプールとしてまとめて扱えるようになり、一時的な高負荷でも保護回路が誤作動しにくくなります！

2️⃣ nvidia-smiで電力制限（パワーリミット）をかける
コマンドラインから `sudo nvidia-smi -pl 400` を実行し、グラフィックボードの最大消費電力（TGP）の上限を400W〜450W程度に抑えます。これでスパイクの最大値そのものを安全なレベルまで下げられます。

3️⃣ 超大容量電源へのアップグレード
ATX 3.0規格の1200W電源でも耐えきれない場合があるため、過渡応答性能に優れたSeasonicなどの1600Wクラスの超大容量電源へリプレイスするのも非常に有効なアプローチです。

せっかく手に入れた最高峰のGPUですから、足回りの電源環境もしっかり整えて、安全で快適なローカルAIライフを送りましょう！

content:
Andrej Karpathy just admitted his best prompting technique is being lazy on purpose

When he can't quite articulate what he wants, he doesn't carefully craft a prompt. He switches to voice and rambles. Unstructured, unedited, stream of consciousness, for a full 10 minutes

No outline. No "let me organize my thoughts first." Just talks until it's out of his head

Turns out LLMs are weirdly great at finding the signal in a mess of half-formed thoughts, and the summary it hands back is often clearer than what you'd have written on purpose

The loop:
→ Ramble for 10 min, total chaos, anything goes
→ Let the model reconstruct what you actually meant
→ Clarify and correct only what's off
→ Repeat until it clicks

His reasoning: thinking out loud beats overthinking in silence, and messy input still beats no input at all

The whole "perfect prompt" obsession might be solving the wrong problem. Sometimes you don't need better prompting. You need to stop editing yourself before you've even finished the thought

For a decade, "text to CAD" meant a party trick: type a prompt, get a blob that vaguely resembled a chair. CAD Skills is the first version that actually ships a part.

9.4k stars. The premise: an agent that designs a mechanical component, sources the hardware for it, and prints it, starting from one sentence.

Prompt it with "80mm flange, 10mm thick, 30mm bore, six bolt holes on a 60mm circle, fillet the outer edges" and it returns a STEP file, the exact format mechanical engineers hand off on real production lines. Not a render. Not a mesh blob. A file SolidWorks and Fusion open natively.

The benchmark folder is the real flex. Same pipeline, one paragraph in, produces: a stepped shaft with a machined keyway. A clevis bracket with lightening cutouts and reinforcing ribs, aerospace-style. 

A radial engine cylinder with 12 cooling fins and an angled spark-plug boss. A centrifugal impeller with 12 backward-curved blades swept from root to tip. A planetary gear stage — sun, planet, ring, carrier — five bodies, correctly assembled. A spiral staircase with a helical handrail wrapping a full revolution. This is the geometry of a mechanical engineering degree, produced from plain English.

And the part is just the input to the next stage, not the finish line:

→ https://t.co/uDBIycauK1 pulls real off-the-shelf hardware — screws, bearings, motors, connectors — so the design isn't floating in isolation
→ URDF and SRDF turn that same geometry into robot description files MoveIt2 and simulators load directly — the part becomes a joint in something that moves
→ SDF builds the physics, sensors, and lighting for the world it moves in
→ the gcode skill slices it with real slicer CLIs, against your actual printer profile
→ Bambu Labs dry-runs the print, uploads it, and starts the job on hardware sitting on your desk

Sentence in. Manufacturable file out. Physical object in your hand. The loop actually closes.

11 skills, MIT licensed, one command to install into Claude Code or Codex.

This is what the "AI designs your hardware" pitch has been promising since 2015. It finally works.

title: European Commission fines AliExpress €550 million for breaching Digital Services Act
content: The European Commission on Monday has fined Chinese online marketplace AliExpress €550 million for failing to assess and reduce risks related to the sale of illegal, unsafe, and counterfeit products on its platform, making it one of the largest penalties ever issued under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) . In commenting on AliExpress’ non-compliance with its statutory responsibilities, Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy stated: “The spread of counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, dangerous cosmetics and other illegal and harmful products is not an unavoidable cost of shopping online, it is a failure by AliExpress to comply with its obligations under the DSA. Scale is not an excuse; risks must be identified and addressed systematically to ensure consumers can safely shop online. Today, we are holding AliExpress to this standard and request it to take action.” The DSA requires platforms with more than 45 million monthly users in the EU to identify and lessen systemic risks, including the spread of illegal content and goods. Under the law, marketplaces are also mandated to conduct the necessary verifications into the information of sellers and make reasonable efforts to authenticate the products sold on their services. Companies found in breach can face penalties of up to 6 percent of their total worldwide annual turnover. The Commission has stated that its investigation found that AliExpress did not take adequate measures to prevent the sale of prohibited items, such as counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, and hazardous cosmetics. Flagged products sometimes remained available for weeks after identification, and the company’s brand authorization verification system was not sophisticated enough to prevent counterfeit listings. title: New EU Court of Justice Ruling on Platform Liability Could Cause Collateral Damage to Freedom of Expression
content: Intermediary liability laws around the world recognize that social media platforms, search engines, and other online service providers have become an integral part of our lives: they shape how we access information, communicate with others and participate in public debate, and foster innovation online. These laws generally shield platforms, to varying degrees, from legal liability for user content: the responsibility for unlawful speech should rest primarily with the speaker, not with those who merely host it. These liability protections are not a gift for platforms. They exist so that platforms are not encouraged to proactively monitor and filter what we say online, or to remove even lawful speech simply to avoid legal risk. This is why a recent judgment by the EU Court of Justice, Coyote System (Joined Cases C-188/24 and C-190/24), is concerning: it could deprive online platforms of liability protection because of how they organize and disseminate user content. The consequences for freedom of expression could be significant. Liability Protections in the EU The European Union has long embraced a system of limited liability for online service providers. Under the e-Commerce Directive and now the Digital Services Act (DSA) , platforms benefit from liability exemptions for user content. To discourage censorship, they also cannot be required to generally monitor user content or actively search for illegal activity. But that liability protection comes with qualifications : Platforms lose this benefit if they play an "active role" such that they have knowledge of, or control over, user-provided information (Recital 42 ECD, Recital 18 DSA, and case law, for example para. 113 in L’Oréal v eBay) . For hosting services, providers must remove or disable content they know to be illegal.
